# Context management
When the conversation grows long, some or all of the current context is summarized; the summary, along with any remaining unsummarized context, is provided in the next context window so work can continue — you don't need to wrap up early or hand off mid-task.

When you have enough information to act, act. Do not re-derive facts already established in the conversation, re-litigate a decision the user has already made, or narrate options you will not pursue. If you are weighing a choice, give a recommendation, not an exhaustive survey

WebSearch takes a `mode`. Use "standard" by default: it is the normal search, quick and cheap. Use "extended" only when a "standard" result comes back thin, off-target or possibly outdated, or from the start for hard-to-find or niche facts, very recent events, prices and availability, and multi-step research: it is thorough and fresh but several times the cost. When you plan several searches, send them in the same turn.

<runtime_info>In case you're asked: you are running in T3 Code through the Claude Code harness. No need to mention this otherwise. You can embed images, video, and audio in your response using Markdown image syntax with absolute file paths. Link any other file you produce using its absolute path so the user can open it in T3 Code's files viewer.</runtime_info>

<pull_request_linking>
Link each PR you create, take over, or push to: one link_pull_request per PR, full URL, every stack layer, as your next call. Host tools do not link for you. If linking fails, say so. Skip PRs you only read or review, and PRs named only as background. Call watch_pull_request when asked to monitor or babysit, or when work you were asked to do, such as a merge, still waits on checks or reviews, even after an earlier unwatch. Finish any needed branch update and push first, then watch and end your turn. Otherwise act now or hand back. Delegated children never watch, even if the brief says babysit. After PR work, a child's last line is: PR <full URL>, head <SHA>, checks and reviews <state>. Links and watches persist across pushes. Never wait with sleep, loops, gh --watch, Monitor, or ScheduleWakeup. Before handback, call unwatch_pull_request on any PR you watch.
</pull_request_linking>

## T3 Code orchestration

Ordinary coding tasks need no T3 tools.

- Subagents: use your native tool when the child uses your provider, a model it offers, and no settings beyond yours, and it finishes in this turn (Claude `Agent` always with `run_in_background:false`; Codex `spawn_agent`, then wait). Use `delegate_task` for another provider's model, user-asked settings, a separate checkout (`isolation:"worktree"`), background work, or `delegate_task` by name. A native type running another provider's model counts too. Workflow only when asked.
- Call `orchestrator_capabilities` once per thread, before the first `delegate_task`. Again only after an error or a user-named provider change. Settings go in `target.options`. Provider or model unavailable: say so. Never switch unasked, or fall back to native tools, Workflow, or CLIs. Never make a child's checkout in the shell or in `task`.
- Every new delegate review or re-check is a new `delegate_task` (brief, findings, objections), never a `t3_thread_send`. Fix small review findings yourself; start no delegate for them. When told to proceed without a delegate, or to run fewer, `task_cancel` the extras. Start no replacement.
- Follow a running delegate's `next`. Do not poll it (`task_status`, `sleep`, watchers, Monitor, ScheduleWakeup). Stop a delegate run you replace or no longer need with `task_cancel`, never `t3_thread_interrupt` on a `childThreadId`.
- If you are a subagent or child, do the work yourself. Start no subagents unless your task says to.

- `t3_thread_launch` and `create_threads` make new top-level threads, only when the user asks for a new thread. "Subagent", "delegate", and "parallel" never mean one. Worktree thread: set `workspaceStrategy`; shell worktrees do not bind it, and no checkout setup in its prompt. No `workspaceStrategy`: project root, not your worktree.
- Given a thread id, `t3_thread_read` it before you answer about it.
- In your reply, a thread's first mention is its `link` verbatim. No `link`: `[title](t3-thread://v1/<exact id>)`. Never a plain title or bare id.
- A secret: call `request_secret` yourself. Pass its `secretRef` to a T3 tool, or use `delivery: "file"` for a shell command. Never ask in chat or invent one. When asked only to schedule, `schedule_task` without running its prompt.
- T3 tools may load late. Try the name once before you call it absent.

### Visuals and preview

- Answer data with a trend or comparison with a chart, and show any visual the user asks for here: pass its HTML to `html_preview`, then `html_render`. If the visual is a file, pass that file's HTML. A screenshot on disk or a text description does not show it. Never start a server for it. Tools a web page exposes give data only. Never use them to show results. Asked for an image to post, send, or use elsewhere: a `.png` file and its path, never `html_render`.
- Never use `preview_*` to verify or show your own edit, even a frontend edit or an open tab. Do not repeat preview calls from an earlier turn. Use them only when the current request asks for browser work or names a page or tab. Public pages: web fetch or search unless browser work was asked; then preview tools only, no web fetch. Close a tab you opened before you reply, unless the user asked for it or uses it.


### Background work you wait on

To wait for a background command or Monitor you started (tests, a build), call `t3_background_wait` with its task ID before you end your turn. Do not mark work you leave running, or PRs. T3 MCP tools are deferred: load one with ToolSearch before you call it.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

**Do not spawn agents unless the user asks.** Each spawn starts cold and re-derives context you already have — it's the expensive path on this plan. A task with "multiple angles," "thorough," or several parts is not a request to spawn; handle it inline with your own tools. Only use this tool when the user explicitly says to use a subagent, or names one of the available agent types.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

The user may see only the question dialog: tool results and text you wrote earlier in this turn may not be on their screen while it is open. Make each question stand on its own: if it depends on something you found, say so briefly, and name the items you are asking about in the question itself.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

This tool runs Git Bash (POSIX sh), not cmd.exe or PowerShell. Use Unix shell syntax: `/dev/null` not `NUL`, forward slashes, `$VAR` not `%VAR%` or `$env:VAR`. Do not use PowerShell here-strings (`@'…'@`) or backtick continuation here — for multi-line strings use a heredoc.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)

tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch

Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

I'm checking the Codex skills directory structure and confirming whether Codex reads from ~/.agents/skills at the user scope plus repo-level .agents/skills. I also want to verify whether the project's .claude/skills entries are real directories or symlinks, and check for provenance files and the repo's missing .agents folder alongside the synced claude skills directory.

I'm also looking at the .codex/skills contents, the skill-lock file, whether these are tracked by git, and any cached plugin skills within codex plugins.

input.command:
$h=$env:USERPROFILE
"=== project .claude/skills detail"; Get-ChildItem .claude\skills -Force | % { "{0}`t{1}`t{2}" -f $_.Name, $(if($_.LinkType){"LINK->"+$_.Target}else{"dir"}), $(if($_.PSIsContainer){(Get-ChildItem $_.FullName -Recurse -File | Measure -Property Length -Sum).Sum}else{$_.Length}) }
"=== git tracked"; git ls-files .claude .agents .codex | Select -First 5; git ls-files .claude | Measure | % Count
"=== provenance"; Get-Content .claude\skills\p3-PROVENANCE.md -TotalCount 40
"=== .claude/skills/synced"; Get-ChildItem "$h\.claude\skills\synced" -Force | Select -Expand Name
"=== codex skills"; Get-ChildItem "$h\.codex\skills" -Recurse -Depth 2 -Directory | Select -Expand FullName
"=== codex config"; Get-Content "$h\.codex\config.toml" | Select-String -Pattern 'skill|plugin|\[' | Select -First 60
"=== other gitignore"; git check-ignore -v .claude/skills 2>&1

content.text:
# Skill layout and cleanup recommendations

I only read files. Nothing has been changed.

## Where everything lives

| Location | Read by | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.agents/skills/` (git repo, `squidllee/skills`) | Codex natively. Claude only through links. | 66 skills, the canonical global store |
| `~/.claude/skills/` | Claude, globally | 8 links into `~/.agents`: `babysit-pr`, `council`, `file-pr`, `full-send`, `full-stop`, `leaving-pr-comments`, `modernize`, `takeover`. It also holds 5 real copies of `here-now` and `instabox*`, a `visualize` folder, a `synced/` folder (~16 MB) and `smol-loop.lnk`. |
| `~/.claude/commands/` | Claude | 3 links into `~/.agentskills`: `canvas-design`, `frontend-design`, `web-artifacts-builder` |
| Claude plugins | Claude | `frontend-design` and `rust-analyzer-lsp` |
| `~/.codex/skills/` | Codex | `.system` (imagegen, openai-docs, skill-creator and others), `codex-primary-runtime` (slides, spreadsheets), `hatch-pet` |
| `~/.codex/plugins/cache/` | Codex | Plugin skills: superpowers (14), expo (13), slack (6), google-calendar (5), github (4), build-web-apps (5), linear, visualize, computer-use, adobe, pets, plus stale `plugin-backup-*` folders |
| `inkling/.claude/skills/` (tracked in git) | Claude, in this repo only | 29 skills. Codex can't see them. |
| `inkling/.agents/skills`, `inkling/.codex` | Codex, in this repo | These don't exist. Codex in inkling sees only the global skills. |

Commit `5f93d48` moved the project skills from `.agents/` to `.claude/`. That is why Codex lost them in this repo.

## Duplicates

**1. 23 skills exist in both `~/.agents` and `inkling/.claude/skills`.**
- 14 are identical copies: `animaxxing` (about 540 KB), `animaxxing-webgl`, `style-animaxxing`, `gsap-core`, `gsap-react`, `address-findings`, `merge`, `unslop`, and 6 `principle-*` skills.
- 8 have drifted. The project copies were edited on 10/27, the global ones on 10/14. Neither side is strictly newer:
  - `principle-fix-root-causes`, `principle-make-operations-idempotent` and `principle-test-behavior-not-implementation` are reworded in the project.
  - `principle-type-system-discipline` is trimmed in the project, which dropped 4 bullets.
  - `maintain-verification-skill` is adapted to this repo's paths.
  - `technical-writing`, `typescript-best-practices` and `using-entire` have small tweaks.

**2. Five real directories in `~/.claude/skills` are byte-identical to `~/.agents`.** These are `here-now` and the four `instabox*` skills. Every other global skill there is a link, so these should be links too.

**3. Overlapping purposes.**
- `babysit` (project) and `babysit-pr` (global) do the same job.
- `run-review` (global) and `review` (project) overlap.
- `leaving-pr-comments` (global) and `pr-comment` (project) overlap. The project one is the newer shape.
- Codex's `visualize` plugin and Claude's `~/.claude/skills/visualize` serve the same purpose.
- Codex's `superpowers` bundle overlaps with your own `principle-*`, `sharpen` and `merge` skills.

## Recommendations

**Make project-specific. These skills are inkling-only or useful in few other places:**
- `verify-inkling`, `land` and `maintain-verification-skill` are already project-only, apart from the global copy of `maintain-verification-skill`. Delete that global copy, since it points at the wrong paths.
- `animaxxing`, `animaxxing-webgl`, `style-animaxxing`, `gsap-core` and `gsap-react` are the biggest weight. Keep them in the project only if inkling actually uses GSAP. If it doesn't, delete them from the project. The global store already has `gsap-core`, `gsap-react` and `gsap-timeline`/`gsap-scrolltrigger`/`gsap-plugins`/`gsap-utils`/`gsap-performance`/`gsap-vanilla`, so `animaxxing` and `style-animaxxing` are the only ones worth keeping local.
- `principle-subtract-before-you-add` exists only in the project. It fits your "yagni" stance, so consider promoting it to global (see below).

**Make global. These aren't inkling-specific:**
- `babysit`, `merge`, `address-findings`, `review` and `pr-comment` are generic PR workflow skills. They belong in `~/.agents/skills`, linked into `~/.claude/skills`.
- The 12 `principle-*` skills, `unslop`, `technical-writing` and `typescript-best-practices` are general. They are in the project only because Claude doesn't read `~/.agents`.
- `using-entire` is also generic.

**The root problem is that Claude can't read `~/.agents/skills` directly.** It only sees what's linked into `~/.claude/skills`. So the project holds copies of skills you want everywhere. The fix is to link all the general skills into `~/.claude/skills` (as you already did for 8), and then delete the project copies. That leaves one source of truth and removes the drift.

**Prune outright:**
- The stale `plugin-backup-*` folders in the Codex plugin cache.
- Unused Codex plugins: `expo`, `google-calendar`, `slack` and `adobe`, unless you use them.
- `~/.claude/skills/synced/` (16 MB). Check first what it is.
- `handle-codebase-scan`, which is already deleted in the `~/.agents` working tree but not committed.
- Skills listed in `.skill-lock.json` whose folders are gone. Roughly 40 entries point at skills you already pruned.

**To keep Codex working in inkling,** either add a `.agents/skills` link to `.claude/skills` in the repo, or rely on the global store once the project copies are removed.

## Decision for you

Do you want one source of truth in `~/.agents/skills` linked into Claude, with only inkling-specific skills (`verify-inkling`, `land`, the animaxxing set if used) left in the repo? That is my recommendation. Before I touch anything, I need you to confirm two things:
- Which version of the 8 drifted skills should win, the project edits or the global ones?
- Whether inkling really uses GSAP and the animaxxing skills.

### Ported

- **New skill `ketchup`** (978ca6e, ea32d95). Catches the user up on everything since their last message, with an executive summary per action item. Before/after visuals use `preview_*`/`device_screenshot` captures and `html_preview` + `html_render` collages. State is read with `list_thread_pull_requests`, `task_status`, and `t3_thread_read`.
- **`p3-help`** (00b52d9, 807c031, 1e56b29). Typed-only (`disable-model-invocation: true`). New `references/prompting.md` and `references/recipes.md`, with `/loop` rewritten as "run until done". Asks once per thread about `/setup-p3` when `p3-models.md` is missing. Adds a `/ketchup` row and a `/ketchup` vs `/recall` close call.
- **The thread runs `/p3-mode`, and `p3-agent` is only a delegate** (2bd5dd4). Applied in `p3-mode/SKILL.md` and `agents/p3-agent.md`.
- **`worktree-cleanup`** (cf9a111, 08bd59b). Judge merge state against the default branch (`origin/HEAD`, then `origin/main`, then `origin/master`) or the PR target, after fetching it. Upstream fixed this in `worktree-audit.sh`; p3 carries it as prose. Intro cut.
- **`create-verification-skill`** (c49b37a). Ready means usable from an empty data dir, not a port answering. An unsatisfiable journey reports failure with the reason in Gotchas. Setup done only by a stand-in stays unverified until the real target is run.
- **`unslop`** (bc697d0). "Must always apply." is dropped from the description.
- **`setup-p3`** (df58112). The budget-to-effort map is now unlimited/large/medium/small → max/xhigh/high/medium, and the default budget is `large (xhigh)`.
- **Token-cutting distillation** (00b14f1, 08bd59b), carried through with T3 wiring kept:
  - `p3-mode`: principle leaf names and playbook paths derived from titles.
  - `babysit`, `opening-a-pr`, `trace-forensics`.
  - `architect` (+ runner prompt), `arena`, `benchmark-checklist`, `blast-radius`, `figure-it-out`, `technical-writing`.
  - `how` (+ explorer prompt), `interrogate` (+ reviewer prompt, rubric), `reflect` (+ all four reviewer/synthesizer prompts).
  - `why` (+ epistemics, investigator and synthesizer prompts, and the code-archaeology, datadog, incident-postmortem, sentry and slack sources).
  - Thirteen principles: build-the-lever, encode-lessons-in-structure, exhaust-the-design-space, explain-the-number, guard-the-context-window, laziness-protocol, minimize-reader-load, model-the-domain, never-block-on-the-human, redesign-from-first-principles, subtract-before-you-add, test-behavior-not-implementation, type-system-discipline.
135:- **Shipping cut to six steps** (ce649c0). After a merge, the child PR is retargeted to trunk, its patch moves onto the merge result, and it is pushed with `--force-with-lease`; the patch-id rule decides whether its verdict survives. `opening-a-pr` points stacked children at that step. T3 wiring

content.text:
Not really. The symlink is the smallest option, and the alternatives are all worse for this repo.

| Option | Problem |
|---|---|
| One tracked symlink (current) | On a Windows machine that can't create symlinks, it checks out as a text file. Codex then sees nothing there, and nothing else breaks. |
| Real files in `.agents/skills`, symlink for `.claude/skills` | Same symlink weakness, with Claude as the one affected. Claude is the main tool here, so that's worse. `verify-inkling` also hardcodes `.claude/skills/...` paths. |
| Real copies in both folders | There are only two skills at about 29 KB, but the copies would drift. Keeping them in sync needs a script or CI check, which is more machinery than one link. |
| Rewrite the skills to be path-agnostic and copy them | Same drift problem as plain copies. |

Windows only creates symlinks with Developer Mode or admin rights. You already depend on that: every link in `~/.claude/skills` is a symlink, and so was the `.agents/skills` link I just made.

I'd keep the symlink. The failure case is a second Windows machine without symlink rights. Even there, Claude is unaffected and only Codex loses the project skills. I'd only switch to copies plus a check if you start cloning this repo onto machines like that.
